AccountingPeriodSelect.name: AccountingPeriodSelect
AccountingPeriodSelect.description:
Accounting month picker.

Kept separate from `PeriodPicker` because it solves a different problem:
payroll is not calculated "from the 3rd to the 17th", but for a month. The
value is therefore `{ year, month }`, not a date range — and code that uses
it cannot accidentally end up with half a month.

props.name: minDate
props.description: Earliest month offered — usually the date the ledger was opened.

AchievementBadge.name: AchievementBadge
AchievementBadge.description:
Achievements.

Business software is dry, and the work inside it is repetitive and largely
invisible - nobody notices a bookkeeper who cleared the queue, only one who
did not. An achievement says the work was seen.

Follows the GitHub pattern: the badge is an IMAGE the application supplies, not
an icon from a set. That is the line between a design system and a product -
the system frames, crops, dims and labels the badge; what is drawn on it is the
product's decision, and a customer will want their own.

Three rules the component enforces, and each is about not doing harm:

A locked achievement shows WHAT is required, not just that it is locked. A grey
square with no explanation is a taunt, not a goal.

Progress is shown where it exists. "6 of 10" is something a person can act on
today; "not yet earned" is not.

A locked badge is DIMMED, never hidden. A goal nobody can see is not a goal.

props.name: withTooltip
props.description: Turns off the tooltip when the name is already written beside the badge.

AchievementGrid.name: AchievementGrid
AchievementGrid.description: Achievements as cards, with names, level and progress.

props.name: cols
props.type: { base: number; sm?: number; lg?: number; }

ActionButton.name: ActionButton
ActionButton.description:
A button described by intent, not by appearance.

Deliberately does NOT accept `color`, `variant`, or `leftSection`. Those
three props are the reason two screens in the same application look like
two products. Color, weight, and icon are a consequence of what the button
does.

The label can be changed — "New person" instead of "New" is more precise
and useful. The color cannot.

props.name: disabledReason
props.description:
Why the button is disabled.

A disabled button with no explanation is a dead end: the user sees they
cannot proceed, but does not know what to do. When this is passed, the
tooltip also works on the disabled button.

props.name: iconOnly
props.description: Hides the label and leaves only the icon; the label moves into the description.

props.name: label
props.description: A more precise label — "New person" instead of "New". The color does not change.

props.name: primary
props.description:
Raises the weight to `filled` regardless of the default.
Used only for the screen's primary action.

props.name: shortcut
props.description: Shown in the description and next to the label; e.g. `['Ctrl', 'N']`.

ActionGroup.name: ActionGroup
ActionGroup.description:
Group of buttons with consistent spacing.

Exists so the spacing between actions is the same everywhere — not 4px on
one screen and 12px on another because one person used `Group gap="xs"`
and another `"sm"`.

props.name: align
props.description:
Alignment. Right by default.

The primary action sits on the right because that is where the eye
expects it at the end of a form, and on a phone that is where the thumb
is too. Left is used only when the group sits next to text.

ActiveStatusBadge.name: ActiveStatusBadge
ActiveStatusBadge.description: Icon to the left of the text - useful when color alone carries meaning.

ApprovalChain.name: ApprovalChain
ApprovalChain.description:
Approval chain.

Who confirmed, who is next, who rejected and why. The same pattern covers
invoice approval, a payment order, a KYC decision, and vacation approval.

The justification is shown only when it exists, but on rejection the
absence of a justification is a sign of a process error — that is why it is
visually highlighted.

props.name: requiresAll
props.description: When `true`, everyone must approve; otherwise one is enough.

AppShellTemplate.name: AppShellTemplate
AppShellTemplate.description:
Application chrome: header, navigation, breadcrumbs, user menu.

Knows nothing about routing — it receives the path and the active address
as data. Because of this, the same shell works in Liro Business App, ERP,
and CRM, and only `navigation` in `LiroAppProvider` and the content differ.

props.name: breadcrumbs
props.description: Path to the current page; the application computes it from its router.

props.name: contentWidth
props.description: Content measure. Side padding is a system decision, not a page one.

props.name: navigationMode
props.description:
How the main navigation is displayed.

`tabs` is the default and recommended: tabs in the header leave all the
space below for content, and the user sees every part of the application
at a glance. A sidebar takes up 260px of width on every screen forever,
which is not a small price on a table with twelve columns.

`sidebar` exists for applications with more than about ten sections.

props.name: onSearch
props.description: Opens search (Spotlight or a custom one). Without it, the button is not shown.

props.name: pathname
props.description: Current address — used to highlight the active navigation item.

ArticleCard.name: ArticleCard
ArticleCard.description:
Article card: a photo in the background, a title over it.

Text over a photo is the one contrast case `axe` CANNOT measure — it does
not read the photo, so it reports `incomplete`, not a failure. The test
passes and the problem stays. That is why the darkening is not a matter of
taste:

  white on 45% black over a WHITE image  = 3.35   fails
  white on 55% black over a WHITE image  = 4.76   passes

`surface.scrim` is 55% and is calculated for the worst case. The image does
not know how light it is, so the lightest possible one is assumed.

props.name: image
props.description: Path to the image. Goes in as a CSS background, so decoration — the title carries the meaning.

props.name: title
props.description: Article title. Data, not a system label — hence `string`.

props.name: action
props.description: Action at the bottom, when `href` is NOT given. With `href` it would be a nested link.

props.name: category
props.description: Section, tag, date. Sits above the title, in caps.

props.name: href
props.description:
When given, the ENTIRE card is a link.

This is deliberate instead of a button in the corner: one target for the
mouse and the keyboard, and the link's accessible name is the title. A
card with a title and a separate button gives two targets that lead to
the same place.

AttachmentList.name: AttachmentList
AttachmentList.description: List of attachments, opened through a signed URL, with removal.

props.name: canRemove
props.description:
Which attachments may be removed.

The rule this exists for is an accounting one: **an attachment cannot be
deleted once the document is posted**, because at that point it is evidence.

Before this prop, the application enforced it by not passing `onRemove` at
all - which removed deletion from the whole list rather than from one file,
and put a domain rule in the screen instead of in the component.

Omitting it means every attachment may be removed, which is the right
default for a draft.

AuditTrail.name: AuditTrail
AuditTrail.description:
Record history. In business software this is often the most important
panel on screen — when something goes wrong, the first question is who
did what and when.

AuthShell.name: AuthShell
AuthShell.description:
Screen for sign-in, password recovery, and two-factor verification.

The form is always on the left and always a fixed width of 360px. The
photo is decoration and disappears below the `sm` breakpoint — on a phone
it does not compete with the fields.

props.name: cover
props.description:
Image on the right side. Pass a `next/image` element for it to be
optimized; if omitted, the form takes the full width.

props.name: footer
props.description: Text below the form - terms of use, version, contact.

AutoForm.name: AutoForm
AutoForm.description:
A form described by a schema.

Values are read through `useWatch` only where a field genuinely depends on
another. Watching the whole form on every change is the most common reason
a form with forty fields starts lagging behind typing.

props.name: defaultValues
props.description: Filled in means an edit, empty means a new entry.

props.name: footer
props.description: Extra content between the fields and the buttons.

props.name: formError
props.description: Message that applies to the whole record, not to a single field.

props.name: serverErrors
props.description:
Errors returned by the server, by field.

Client-side validation is never complete: PIB uniqueness, rules only the
database knows, checks on another system. When the server says which
field is wrong, the error must sit next to that field — a general message
at the top does not connect to the input and the user has to hunt for
their mistake.

Passed in from `fieldErrorsOf(error)` in `@liro/data`.

props.name: validationSchema
props.description:
Schema for the whole record — Zod, Valibot, or anything that implements
Standard Schema.

Rules from `FieldSchema` (`required`, `validate`) still apply and run
BEFORE the schema, so existing forms keep working unchanged. The schema
adds what a single field cannot know on its own: relationships between
fields and rules shared with the server.

An error with no path applies to the whole record and is shown in the bar
at the top.

props.name: withoutActions
props.description: Hides the button bar — when the form lives in a modal with its own footer.

BrandMark.name: BrandMark
BrandMark.description:
Wordmark in the brand typeface. The only place Space Grotesk appears —
if it shows up anywhere else, that is a bug.

props.name: name
props.description: Overrides the name from `LiroAppProvider`.

props.name: responsive
props.description: When `false`, always shows the full name with no responsive swap.

props.name: shortName
props.description: Shorter name shown below the `sm` breakpoint.

BulkActionBar.name: BulkActionBar
BulkActionBar.description:
Bar of actions over selected rows.

Appears above the table when something is checked and disappears when it
is not. Deliberately pushes content down instead of floating over it: a bar
floating at the bottom of the screen covers the last row exactly when the
user is checking what they selected.

props.name: totalCount
props.description: Total number of rows matching the filter — for "select all N".

Callout.name: Callout
Callout.description:
A message inside the page flow - explanation of a rule, deadline warning,
consequence of an action.

Differs from a notification in that it doesn't disappear. Content the user
must read before continuing must not be transient.

props.name: actions
props.description: Actions at the bottom - usually a single `ActionButton`.

CapacityTimeline.name: CapacityTimeline
CapacityTimeline.description:
Capacity distribution over time.

The previous version took shares from 0 to 1 and had no date axis. That
felt flexible, but it forced the application to compute positions itself,
and left the user without an answer to the most important question —
"when, exactly".

Now the component takes REAL dates and computes the layout itself. In
return it gained what was missing: an axis with ticks, a marker for
today, a scale switch, horizontal scroll independent from the label
column, and overlaps shown across multiple lanes instead of one bar over
another.

props.name: from
props.description: Start of the displayed range.

props.name: to
props.description: End of the displayed range, inclusive.

props.name: labelWidth
props.description: Width of the resource-name column.

props.name: withScaleControl
props.description: Shows a scale switch above the axis.

CardMultiSelect.name: CardMultiSelect
CardMultiSelect.description:
Selection via cards instead of radio buttons.

Five options in a radio group is a list to be read. Five cards with an icon
are recognized at a glance — and that is a difference that is felt when the
user opens the same screen a hundred times a day.

Underneath is a real `<input type="radio">`, just visually hidden. That
gives, for free, what is hard to get exactly right with `<div onClick>`:
arrow-key movement within the group, selection with Space, grouping for a
screen reader, and behavior inside a `<form>`.

When an option's description is longer than two sentences, this is not the
right component — the card stops being recognizable at a glance and
becomes a paragraph.

props.name: error
props.description: Error message; shown below the group and colors the border.

props.name: max
props.description: Maximum number of selections allowed; beyond that, the rest are disabled.

CardSelect.name: CardSelect
CardSelect.description:
Selection via cards instead of radio buttons.

Five options in a radio group is a list to be read. Five cards with an icon
are recognized at a glance — and that is a difference that is felt when the
user opens the same screen a hundred times a day.

Underneath is a real `<input type="radio">`, just visually hidden. That
gives, for free, what is hard to get exactly right with `<div onClick>`:
arrow-key movement within the group, selection with Space, grouping for a
screen reader, and behavior inside a `<form>`.

When an option's description is longer than two sentences, this is not the
right component — the card stops being recognizable at a glance and
becomes a paragraph.

props.name: error
props.description: Error message; shown below the group and colors the border.

ChartCard.name: ChartCard
ChartCard.description:
Frame for every chart.

Exists because of three states that in practice always get forgotten:
loading, an empty period, and an error. An empty chart with no explanation
looks like a broken screen — the user does not know whether there is no
data or something broke.

The title, period, and total figure always sit in the same place, so two
charts next to each other read as a pair, not as two separate cards.

props.name: actions
props.description: Period picker, chart-type switch, export.

props.name: footnote
props.description: Note below the chart — data source, method of calculation.

props.name: isEmpty
props.description: When there is no data, the chart is not drawn — an explanation is shown.

props.name: period
props.description: Period the chart covers - "March 2026" or "Last 12 months".

props.name: total
props.description: Summary figure next to the title — most often the total for the period.

Checklist.name: Checklist
Checklist.description:
Checklist of checks.

One component covers a client KYC/AML check, quality control on a
manufacturing order, incoming goods inspection, and a documentation audit —
because in all four cases it is a set of checks with an outcome and
evidence.

`blocking` exists because not all checks are equal: one unfinished blocking
check means the whole set has not passed, regardless of the others.

props.name: withSummary
props.description: Shows a progress bar and a total above the list.

CodeBlock.name: CodeBlock
CodeBlock.description:
Code display.

In a business application this is not decoration — it is used for XML
filings (PPP-PD, PP OD-O), SEF's JSON responses, and request bodies in the
integration log. When something fails, the bookkeeper and the developer
look at the same screen, so readability and the ability to copy are not
optional.

props.name: maxHeight
props.description: Limits the height; long files get scroll instead of an endless page.

props.name: withLineNumbers
props.description: Shows line numbers — required for XML sent to the tax authority.

CodeBlockTabs.name: CodeBlockTabs
CodeBlockTabs.description: Multiple files in tabs — e.g. the request and response of one integration.

CommandPalette.name: CommandPalette
CommandPalette.description:
Command palette - `Ctrl+K`.

Exists because human behavior does not change: someone entering data all
day does not take their hands off the keyboard to hunt for a menu. The
palette brings navigation and actions into one place, so any screen is
reached by typing its name.

Navigation is taken from `LiroAppProvider` and is already filtered through
permissions, so the palette cannot offer a screen the user has no right to.

props.name: actions
props.description: Actions tied to the current screen.

props.name: withNavigation
props.description: When `false`, navigation is not shown in the palette.

CommentThread.name: CommentThread
CommentThread.description:
Correspondence attached to a record — comments on a document, messages to
a client, a bookkeeper's notes.

Other people's messages sit on the left, your own on the right, system
messages in the middle. People recognize this layout from every messaging
application they have ever used, so it needs no explanation.

props.name: layout
props.description:
`bubbles` is a conversation: sides left and right, a corner toward the
sender. `flat` is a remark on a document: no bubble, the body indented
under the name.

In the `flat` form, `own` does NOT align right. In correspondence, who is
speaking matters; in a list of remarks, what is written matters — and a
long remark aligned right is harder to read for no benefit.

ConfirmModal.name: ConfirmModal
ConfirmModal.description:
General action confirmation. Not tied to deletion - see `DeleteConfirmModal`
below for that case, which just fills in the default texts.

props.name: confirmColor
props.description: Color of the Mantine confirm button; defaults to following `tone`.

ConflictBanner.name: ConflictBanner
ConflictBanner.description:
Concurrent-edit conflict.

The default way out is reloading, not overwriting — because at that
moment the user does not know what the other side changed. `onOverwrite`
exists for cases where the application knows it is safe, but it is never
offered as the first choice and is never highlighted.

props.name: changedBy
props.description: Who changed the record, if known.

props.name: fields
props.description: Fields that differ - shown side by side.

DangerZoneCard.name: DangerZoneCard
DangerZoneCard.description:
Irreversible actions, kept separate from the rest of the settings.

The red border and its own card exist so that this button does not end up
next to the theme switch — the difference in consequence must be visible
even before reading.

props.name: canDelete
props.description: When `false`, deletion is disabled with an explanation.

DashboardTemplate.name: DashboardTemplate
DashboardTemplate.description: Module home page: figures at the top, content below.

DataTable.name: DataTable
DataTable.description:
A table with not a single call to the database.

Takes rows and returns events — sorting, selection, row click, actions. That
way the same table works on top of Supabase, a REST API, or an in-memory
array. The layer that fetches data is `ResourceTable` in `@liro/data`, and
it just wraps this one.

props.name: footer
props.description: Row of totals at the bottom. Sticks to the bottom edge while scrolling.

props.name: isFetching
props.description: Data is refreshing, but the old row is still on screen.

props.name: isRowSelectable
props.description: Disables selection of an individual row — e.g. an already-posted document.

props.name: maxHeight
props.description: Height of the scroll container when `virtualized`.

props.name: mobile
props.description:
Phone display. A table with six columns on a 380px screen is unusable no
matter how well it scrolls — that is why below `sm` every row renders as a
card.

Without this configuration, the first column is used as the title, the
second as the subtitle, and the rest as label/value pairs.

props.name: resizableColumns
props.description:
Lets the user drag column widths.

Off by default. A resizable column needs a fixed table layout, which changes
how every column is measured - so it is a decision the screen makes, not a
behaviour every table gets.

Useful where one column holds long text the reader wants to see: an account
name, a description, a client. Not useful on five short columns.

Widths live in the component and reset when the column set changes. They are
deliberately not persisted - remembering them per user is an application
concern and needs somewhere to store them.

props.name: rowHeight
props.description: Height of a single row in pixels when `virtualized`.

props.name: selected
props.description:
Selected rows — controlled. The checkbox column appears only when BOTH
props are passed.

The application holds them because the selection, as a rule, survives a
page change: the user checks three IOS statements on the first page, two
on the third, and then runs bulk processing over all five.

props.name: skeletonRows
props.description: Number of skeleton rows while the first load is in progress.

props.name: stickyFirstColumn
props.description:
The first column (and the checkbox, if present) stay visible during
horizontal scroll. For tables with many columns, where without this you
lose track of which row is which.

props.name: virtualized
props.description:
Renders only the rows that are in the viewport.

Turn on only once the list is genuinely large — the chart of accounts has
932 rows and without this creates 932 DOM nodes. Under a few hundred rows,
virtualization is pure overhead.

Condition: all rows must be the same height. Content that wraps onto two
lines will overlap — in that case increase `rowHeight` or turn off
virtualization.

DateRangeText.name: DateRangeText
DateRangeText.description: Also shows the weekday in the hover tooltip.

DateText.name: DateText
DateText.description:
Date as text.

Always `DD.MM.YYYY.` with a trailing dot — that is how dates are written
in Serbian documents. An empty value is a dash, never blank space, so
there is a visible difference between "no date" and "did not load".

props.name: withWeekday
props.description: Also shows the weekday in the hover tooltip.

DeleteConfirmModal.name: DeleteConfirmModal
DeleteConfirmModal.description: Color of the Mantine confirm button; defaults to following `tone`.

props.name: confirmColor
props.description: Color of the Mantine confirm button; defaults to following `tone`.

props.name: text

DetailDrawer.name: DetailDrawer
DetailDrawer.description:
Detail of one record, beside the list it came from.

Exists to preserve context. A user reading a hundred invoices clicks one; a
full page loses the table, the scroll position, the filter and the place in
the list, and getting back costs a navigation. A panel keeps all of it: look,
approve, close, carry on down the table.

Different from `FormDrawer`, which is a form. This is a READING view - the
actions are on it, but the fields are not edited here. When the record needs
editing, the drawer's action navigates to the page: a long form needs an
address, and a drawer has none.

props.name: actions
props.description: Actions at the bottom, always visible.

props.name: onPrevious
props.description:
Moving through the list without closing.

This is what makes the component worth having. Without it the user closes
the panel, finds the next row, and opens it again - which is the navigation
the panel was supposed to remove.

props.name: subtitle
props.description: Second line under the title: a number, a status, a date. Already formatted.

DetailPageTemplate.name: DetailPageTemplate
DetailPageTemplate.description:
Detail page: title with a status badge, content, and an optional side
column. The side column drops below the content on narrow screens.

props.name: aside
props.description: A narrow column shown next to the content — metadata, history, attachments.

props.name: asideSpan
props.description: Width of the side column in Mantine grid columns (out of 12).

DueDate.name: DueDate
DueDate.description:
Due date with status.

Exists because "15.03.2026." on its own is a useless piece of data in a
list of two hundred invoices — the operator needs to see what has been
breached, not do the math in their head. The number of overdue days is in
the tooltip, so it does not create noise in the column.

props.name: settled
props.description: When settled, the deadline is shown neutrally regardless of the date.

props.name: warningDays
props.description: Threshold in days for a warning before expiry; defaults to 5.

EditableGrid.name: EditableGrid
EditableGrid.description:
Grid for row-by-row entry.

Intended for a journal entry, an invoice line breakdown, and everything else
where line items are typed, not picked from a dialog. The entire input must
be possible without a mouse.

Movement:
  Enter        next row, same column; on the last row creates a new one
  Shift+Enter  previous row
  Tab          next cell (left to the browser)

The arrow keys are deliberately NOT taken over: in a number field they
change the value, in text they move the cursor. Taking them over would
remove behavior the user already expects.

props.name: createRow
props.description: Creates an empty row. Called on Enter in the last row and by the button.

props.name: minRows
props.description: Below this number, a row cannot be deleted.

props.name: onBalanceChange
props.description: Reports to the application whether the entry can be saved. The difference is in minor units.

EmptyState.name: EmptyState

props.name: variant

FieldList.name: FieldList
FieldList.description: Filled in means an edit, empty means a new entry.

FileDropzone.name: FileDropzone
FileDropzone.description:
Drag-and-drop attachments.

Uploading goes through `FileStorage` from `@liro/data`, the same as
`UploadField` in forms — so the application configures storage once and it
applies everywhere.

Multiple files are uploaded in sequence, not in parallel. Ten statements
sent at once can bring down the connection on a weaker office internet
line, and a partial failure is worse than a slow success because you
cannot see what went through.

props.name: maxSize
props.description: Maximum size per file in bytes.

ForbiddenTemplate.name: ForbiddenTemplate
ForbiddenTemplate.description:
Interrupted screens. All of them share the same frame from
`StatusScreen` — wordmark, icon in the status color, title, explanation,
one or two actions.

The texts explain what happened and what the user can do. They do not
apologize and do not use technical terms: "The page does not exist" is
more usable than "404 Not Found".

props.name: action
props.description: Overrides the default primary action.

props.name: linkComponent
props.description: Pass `next/link` so returning home stays client-side.

FormDrawer.name: FormDrawer
FormDrawer.description:
Same as `FormModal`, but from the side. Chosen when the form has many
fields or when the user needs to see the list behind it while entering data.

FormField.name: FormField
FormField.description:
Translates a single schema field into a Mantine control.

All fields go through react-hook-form's `Controller`, so behavior (touch,
error, reset) doesn't differ from one type to another.

FormModal.name: FormModal
FormModal.description: Filled in means edit, empty means new entry.

props.name: defaultValues
props.description: Filled in means edit, empty means new entry.

FormWizard.name: FormWizard
FormWizard.description:
A single form split into steps, on a full page.

Difference from `StepWizard` in `@liro/ui`: there the steps are a process
(sign, then submit, then wait for the server); here it is one record filled
in over several sessions. That is why this one has a draft, protection
against leaving with unsaved changes, and a return to the step where the
error is — and that one has none of it.

Three decisions the component enforces:

While going through the steps, only the current one is validated. An error
in a step the user has not yet reached is not an error, just a field not
filled in yet.

On the last step, the whole record is validated. Nothing can pass
unchecked just because the user skipped backward.

When validation fails on an earlier step, the user is taken back there. A
disabled button with no visible reason is the worst possible outcome.

props.name: draftDelay
props.description: Delay in milliseconds before saving the draft.

props.name: draftSavedAt
props.description: Time of the last saved draft; shown in the footer.

props.name: onDirtyChange
props.description: Reports that the form has unsaved changes — for route guarding in the application.

props.name: onDraftChange
props.description:
Called after typing stops, with all values.

Deliberately does not save by itself: the design system does not know
whether the draft goes to Supabase, `localStorage`, or nowhere. When the
prop is not passed, the form does not subscribe to changes and pays
nothing.

props.name: validationSchema
props.description: Schema for the whole record; validated before submitting, not per step.

I18nProvider.name: I18nProvider
I18nProvider.description:
Deliberately neither i18next nor react-intl.

Liro screens carry labels tied to a specific field or column, not to a
global dictionary of keys. When `label` lives next to the column
definition, a translation cannot be forgotten — it is immediately obvious
that one is missing. That is why the unit of translation is an object, not
a key: `{ 'sr-Latn': 'Iznos', en: 'Amount' }`.

props.name: cookieName
props.description: Name of the cookie the language choice is written to.

props.name: initialLocale
props.description:
Pass from the server (e.g. from the user's profile or a cookie).
Never read `localStorage` during initialization — the server would
render one language, the client another, and hydration would break.

props.name: preferences
props.description:
How numbers and dates look, as opposed to what language they are in.

From the user's profile. A bookkeeper in Belgrade running an English interface
still wants `1.234,56` - the language decides what is written, this decides how
it looks.

Passed in rather than stored here, because it lives in the user's profile and
the design system does not own that. Omit it and every user gets the Serbian
defaults.

ItemGallery.name: ItemGallery
ItemGallery.description:
Photos attached to an item.

An article in a warehouse, a room in facility management, equipment, a
sample in quality control — in every case it is a set of photos with a
caption.

Thumbnails are below, not on the side: on a narrow screen, a side strip
cuts the main image in half, and that image is exactly why the gallery is
opened.

props.name: withThumbnails
props.description: Shows thumbnails below the main image.

JobProgress.name: JobProgress
JobProgress.description:
State of a job running on the server.

Bulk processing takes minutes. Without feedback, the user does not know
whether the job is working, how much is left, and what to do when it
fails — so they start it again, and again.

The component does not call the server. The application decides how to
track the job (`useCall` in a loop, Supabase realtime, SSE) and just passes
in the state.

props.description: Error message when the job fails.

props.name: failed
props.description: Number of items that failed — shown even when the job succeeded.

props.description: Processed and total. Without `total`, the bar is indeterminate.

KanbanBoard.name: KanbanBoard
KanbanBoard.description:
Cards in columns, moved between them.

A status flow you can see: invoices awaiting approval, tickets, documents in a
signing queue. The column IS the status, so moving a card is a state change -
which is why `onMove` is the only way anything happens here. The board holds no
state of its own; the application performs the move and sends the cards back.

DRAG IS NOT ACCESSIBLE, and cannot be made so. Neither HTML5 drag-and-drop nor
pointer events reach the keyboard, and the "keyboard drag mode" some libraries
offer is a mode nobody discovers.

So every card carries a "Move to" menu listing the other columns. That is not a
fallback - for a keyboard it is the better path, because it is visible, and it
is the only route for a screen reader. The mouse drags, the keyboard picks from
the menu, both call `onMove`.

Cards are NOT reordered within a column. In a business flow the column is the
status and the order inside it belongs to the application - by date, by
deadline, by amount. Hand-sorting a queue of two hundred invoices is not a thing
anyone does.

props.name: onMove
props.description: The only way a card moves. The application performs it and returns new cards.

Public product landing page.

The layout is deliberately calm: one heading, one sentence of explanation,
two actions. Business software is not sold with exclamation marks but with
clarity about what it does - so the heading is the only place with the
brand typeface, and everything else is readable text at the same scale as
the application itself.

Launchpad.name: Launchpad
Launchpad.description:
Launchpad — tiles.

The shape is carried over from `ModuleGrid` in Liro Business App, down to
the detail: `Paper withBorder radius="md" p="md"`, an icon in a box top
left, a badge top right, a title `size="sm" fw={700}`, below it a
**subtitle**.

Below the title sits a subtitle, not a number. A number felt like a good
idea, but it broke the grid's rhythm — in the original application a tile
is an entry point into a module, not a metric. When a number is needed, it
goes as a badge top right, where `PRO` and `UNAVAILABLE` already sit.

The class is `liro-module-card`, the same as in the original application.
Because of it, the rule `.liro-module-card:hover .liro-module-icon` works,
giving the icon a blue background and white color on hover — previously the
class `liro-tile` was there, so that rule never matched.

props.name: editing
props.description:
Editing mode.

Dragging works ONLY while this is on. Outside of it, tiles are plain
links — otherwise a user who wants to open a module drags it instead of
clicking, which is the most common complaint about boards like this.

The application turns it on with an "Edit layout" button and persists the
order through `onReorder`.

decides what to do with them, the appearance is settled.

props.name: minLength
props.description: Minimum allowed length; defaults to 12.

PdfPositionPicker.name: PdfPositionPicker
PdfPositionPicker.description:
Stamp position picker via dragging over the preview.

Returns coordinates in PDF points with origin bottom-left, because that is
what the signing layer expects — while the screen works in pixels with
origin top-left. The conversion is done here, once, so every application
does not have to do it.

The frame size is only a visual guide; the actual stamp size is computed
by the server. The values should be kept in sync so the user is not
surprised.

props.name: safeMargin
props.description:
Safe zone from every edge of the page, in PDF points.

Home and office printers have a non-printable border of 3 to 6 mm. A stamp
placed inside it is either clipped or printed skewed, and that is discovered
only when someone prints a signed contract.

The default is 10 mm - 28 points at 72 dpi - which covers the worst printer
with room to spare and costs almost nothing on an A4 page. Lower it only for
a known set of printers; the default must be the value that breaks nothing.

props.name: stampWidth
props.description: Stamp size in PDF points — must match the server-side one.

PdfPreview.name: PdfPreview
PdfPreview.description:
PDF preview and stamp position picker.

`pdfjs-dist` is imported DYNAMICALLY, inside an effect, not at the top of
the file.

The reason is not lazy loading but that `pdfjs-dist` uses `DOMMatrix` at
the top level of the module, which only exists in the browser. Next.js
evaluates the module on the server too, even for components with
`'use client'`, so a static import breaks the first render — an error that
is not easy to guess the first time and easy to bring back while cleaning
up imports.

props.name: source
props.description: File from an `input`, an already-read buffer, or a document URL.

props.name: overlay
props.description: Content over the canvas — e.g. the stamp frame.

props.name: page
props.description: Starting page, 1-indexed.

props.name: width
props.description: Display width in pixels; height is computed from the page ratio.

props.name: withZoom
props.description: Zoom controls under the page. On by default.

PeriodPicker.name: PeriodPicker
PeriodPicker.description:
Accounting period picker.

Presets are on the left, the calendar on the right. The order is
deliberate: nine times out of ten the user wants "last month", not to click
two dates. The calendar exists for that tenth time, not as the main path.

When the selected range exactly matches a preset, that preset stays
highlighted — so the label shows whether the period is standard or set
manually.

props.name: clearable
props.description: Allows an empty selection — "all periods".

props.name: presets
props.description: Presets offered; defaults to the eight most common.

PermissionMatrix.name: PermissionMatrix
PermissionMatrix.description:
Roles and permissions matrix.

Exists in every ERP and gets built from scratch everywhere. Two things
that are most often missed, and are built in here: checking a whole group
for one role (otherwise you click forty times) and locked system roles,
which are visible but cannot be changed.

The sticky first column uses the same styles as `DataTable` — hence
`className="liro-table"`. Without it, with about ten roles you lose track
of which row is which permission.

props.name: onChange
props.type: (roleId: string, permissionIds: string[], granted: boolean) => void
props.description: Called for a single cell. Group checking sends multiple calls at once.

props.name: value
props.description: Permissions by role: `value[roleId]` is an array of permission IDs.

props.name: isApplicable
props.description:
Whether a permission applies to a role at all.

Three states, not two: **granted**, **denied**, and **not applicable**.
"Denied" means the role could have this and does not; "not applicable"
means the combination does not exist — deleting a client is not something
a read-only auditor role is ever going to be given.

This is NOT part of `value`. `value` records who may do what; whether a
combination exists is a property of the matrix, derived from the role.
Storing it alongside the grants would mean persisting a fact that is
computed.

A cell that does not apply renders as a dash, never as a disabled
checkbox: a screen reader announces a disabled checkbox as "not granted,
locked", which claims the permission could be granted if something were
unlocked. It cannot. The same rule as "an empty value is a dash" in the
ten rules.

Omitting this means every permission applies to every role.

PersonAvatar.name: PersonAvatar
PersonAvatar.description:
Initials from a name: first letters of the first two words.

NOT `name.slice(0, 2)`. That is the first two CHARACTERS, so "Ana
Jovanovic" gives AN instead of AJ, and "Marko Petrovic" gives MA instead
of MP — in a list of five people, half end up with the same initials.
That mistake existed in two places.

`toUpperCase()` works with both diacritics and Cyrillic: "Đorđe" -> Đ,
"Ана Јовановић" -> АЈ.

props.name: name
props.description: Full name. Initials are derived from it when there is no image.

props.name: alt
props.description:
Name for a screen reader.

By default the avatar is DECORATIVE (`alt=""` + `aria-hidden`), because
in practice the name is always written next to it — in a message, in a
comment, in a table row. Without this, a screen reader reads the name
twice, and the initials "AJ" as a word.

Pass `alt={person.name}` only when the avatar stands ALONE, with no
written name. Then it is the sole carrier of the information.

PersonCard.name: PersonCard
PersonCard.description:
Person card with a colored band in the header and figures.

The header is a COLORED BAND by default, not a photo. Two reasons: visual
regression must not depend on the network, and in a business system a
decorative landscape behind an employee is noise. `coverImage` exists for
when it is genuinely needed.

The action is a slot, not an `intent`-typed prop: the card should not know
about the intent catalog — the application passes
`<ActionButton intent="view" />`.

props.name: position
props.description: Job title or role. Not `role` — that is an ARIA prop, see `PersonInfo`.

PersonCell.name: PersonCell
PersonCell.description:
A person in a table row: avatar, name, and one line underneath.

`minWidth: 0` on the wrapper is required - without it `truncate` doesn't
work inside `Group`, because a flex item by default won't shrink below its
content.

props.name: secondary
props.description: Second line: role, title, department, position.

PersonInfo.name: PersonInfo
PersonInfo.description:
A person with contact details: avatar, role, name, email, and phone.

Contact info is a LINK, not text. A written-out address the user has to
copy by hand is work a computer can do — `mailto:` and `tel:` open the
appropriate app, and on a phone they start a call.

props.name: extra
props.description: Extra rows below the contact info.

props.name: position
props.description:
Job title or role. Sits ABOVE the name, in caps.

NOT `role`: in JSX that prop means an ARIA role, and `jsx-a11y/aria-role`
rejects it on every element — including our own components, not just
the DOM.

PreferencesCard.name: PreferencesCard
PreferencesCard.description:
Account and profile.

These screens exist in every application and are built from scratch
everywhere, so they end up slightly different everywhere. Here they are
components that receive values and return events — the application
decides what to do with them, the appearance is settled.

ProcessDiagram.name: ProcessDiagram
ProcessDiagram.description: React Flow requires its own provider; the wrapper sets it up so the application does not have to.

props.name: editable
props.description: Allows moving nodes — for a process editor.

ProcessMap.name: ProcessMap
ProcessMap.description:
Process map.

Deliberately NOT full BPMN. Full BPMN requires an editor, node layout, pools
and lanes — that is a separate product. This is a readable display of steps
and branches that covers what a diagram is most often drawn for: seeing who
does what and where the record currently is.

Nodes are laid out in array order, and branches are shown as labels on the
connections. When a real BPMN with free layout is needed, this component
gets replaced — the investment in it is small.

ProfileCard.name: ProfileCard
ProfileCard.description:
Account and profile.

These screens exist in every application and are built from scratch
everywhere, so they end up slightly different everywhere. Here they are
components that receive values and return events — the application
decides what to do with them, the appearance is settled.

props.name: emailReadOnly
props.description: Email is most often changed through a separate flow with confirmation.

props.name: errors
props.description: Errors from the server, by field.

ProgressCard.name: ProgressCard
ProgressCard.description:
Card for work in progress: how much is done out of the total.

Deliberately looks like `StatCard` — same header, same icon placement, same
frame. Two cards in the same row should not differ in shape, only in that
one carries a number and the other progress.

props.name: badge
props.description: Badge in the bottom-right corner: deadline, status, warning.

props.name: tone
props.description: Bar color.

props.name: unit
props.description: Unit in the row below the bar: "32 of 47 people".

RateTable.name: RateTable
RateTable.description:
Price list and rate table.

One component for prices by quantity, by period, by guest category, by
sales channel, and by service tier — because all of these are matrices
where the row carries the item and the column the condition.

An empty cell means "not applicable", and is shown as a dash, not as zero.
Zero is a price, a dash is the absence of a price, and those are different
things.

props.name: footnote
props.description: Note below the table — since when it applies, what is not included.

RecordFormTemplate.name: RecordFormTemplate
RecordFormTemplate.description:
Full page for creating and editing a record.

Exists because a form with forty fields does not belong in a modal.

The rule this template enforces:

  full page   an entity with more than about ten fields, with tabs, with
              attachments, or with data read from multiple sources —
              employee, client, contract, entry
  drawer      editing a subset of fields with a list that stays visible —
              a quick price change, assigning a tag
  modal       a short action with one outcome — confirmation, a single
              input, a document preview

The reason is not aesthetics but that a modal has no URL. A long entry
that gets interrupted cannot be resumed, cannot be sent to a colleague, and
does not survive a page refresh. A full page gets all of that for free.

props.name: onBack
props.description: Back to the list. Always present — the user must know how to leave.

props.name: title
props.description: Title: "New person" or the name of the record being edited.

props.name: aside
props.description: Secondary data next to the form — edit history, attachments, help.

props.name: badge
props.description: Status badge next to the title.

props.name: canSubmit
props.description: Disables saving while the form is not valid.

props.name: extraActions
props.description: Extra actions in the header — delete, duplicate, print.

props.name: footnote
props.description: Note above the buttons — what happens upon saving.

props.name: subheader
props.description: Tabs or a progress bar below the title.

RecordStatusBadge.name: RecordStatusBadge
RecordStatusBadge.description:
Record status badge.

Same principle as with buttons: the developer picks the state, not the
color. Draft is always gray, overdue is always red, posted is always
green - across every module and every application.

props.name: label
props.description: A more precise label for a specific module; the color doesn't change.

RelationField.name: RelationField
RelationField.description:
A dropdown that fetches values through `DataProvider`.

Search goes to the server, not through a loaded array. The partner
register in Liro has thousands of rows; fetching all of them when the form
opens is both slow and unnecessary.

props.name: dependencyValue
props.description: Value of the field this list depends on (`relation.dependsOn`).

ResourceTable.name: ResourceTable
ResourceTable.description:
Table connected to a data source.

Assembles `Toolbar`, `DataTable`, and `TablePagination` from `@liro/ui` and
feeds them through `DataProvider`. Display and fetching stay separate:
there is not a single display decision here, and there is not a single
network call in `@liro/ui`.

props.name: resource
props.description: Table or view read from.

props.name: deleteFrom
props.description: When reading from a view with a JOIN, deletion must go to the base table.

props.name: extraActions
props.description: Extra actions in the row menu.

props.name: filterControls
props.description: Filter elements shown in the bar above the table.

props.name: filters
props.description: Filters as a controlled value — the display components live on the application side.

props.name: footer
props.description: Row of totals; values come from the application, not from the current page.

props.name: mobile
props.description: How a row looks as a card on a phone.

props.name: onError
props.description: Displaying the error is the application's responsibility — it knows which notification system it uses.

props.name: searchFields
props.description: Columns free-text search runs over; defaults to all text columns.

props.name: selected
props.description: Selected rows. Held by the application because the selection survives a page change.

props.name: toolbarActions
props.description: Buttons on the right side of the bar.

RichTextField.name: RichTextField
RichTextField.description:
Rich text for notes, service descriptions, and contract clauses.

The toolset is deliberately short. A full editor with colors, sizes, and
fonts in a business application produces documents that look like they were
written by five people — because they were. What exists here is what
carries meaning: bold, italic, headings, lists, quote, and link. Color and
typeface are chosen by the system.

props.name: value
props.description: HTML content.

props.name: readOnly
props.description: No toolbar and no border; used to display saved text.

props.name: toolset
props.description: `minimal` is just bold, italic, and lists — for short notes.

RichTextView.name: RichTextView
RichTextView.description:
Display of saved text without the editor.

Content comes from the database and is rendered as HTML. That is safe only
if it was written through `RichTextField` — if it ever comes from an
external source, it must go through sanitization on the server.

props.name: emptyText
props.description: An empty value produces a dash, not empty space.

RouteProgress.name: RouteProgress
RouteProgress.description:
Progress bar on page navigation.

Next shows `loading.tsx` only once the new route starts loading, and
between the click and that moment there is no feedback at all. On a
slower connection that is half a second in which the user does not know
whether the click registered — so they click again.

The application passes `pathname` from its router; the bar starts on
change and finishes when the new page mounts.

ScoreMeter.name: ScoreMeter
ScoreMeter.description:
Score in a range with zones.

Client risk in AML, creditworthiness, a supplier rating, project health in
research — all of these are a number in a range with decision thresholds.

Zones are described as data because the thresholds differ by regulation and
by company; the component does not assume any of them.

props.name: description
props.description: Explanation of what the score means and where it comes from.

props.name: factors
props.description: Items that contributed to the score.

SectionCard.name: SectionCard
SectionCard.description: Buttons in the top-right corner of the section.

props.name: actions
props.description: Buttons in the top-right corner of the section.

props.name: flush
props.description: Removes inner padding - for sections whose table runs edge to edge.

ServerErrorTemplate.name: ServerErrorTemplate
ServerErrorTemplate.description:
Interrupted screens. All of them share the same frame from
`StatusScreen` — wordmark, icon in the status color, title, explanation,
one or two actions.

The texts explain what happened and what the user can do. They do not
apologize and do not use technical terms: "The page does not exist" is
more usable than "404 Not Found".

props.name: action
props.description: Overrides the default primary action.

props.name: linkComponent
props.description: Pass `next/link` so returning home stays client-side.

SessionsCard.name: SessionsCard
SessionsCard.description: List of signed-in devices. The current one cannot be signed out from here.

ShortcutHint.name: ShortcutHint
ShortcutHint.description:
Shortcut display.

Shortcuts are shown whenever they exist - a user who works in the
application all day learns the ones they see, and never discovers the
ones hidden away in documentation.

props.name: inverted
props.description: For display inside a dark description, where the standard Kbd has no contrast.

SlotPicker.name: SlotPicker
SlotPicker.description:
Free time slot picker.

Reserving a hall, scheduling with an advisor, a machine service slot,
assigning a shift — all of it is picking a free interval on a resource.

The component does NOT compute availability. Free slots arrive from the
server, because only the server knows about other users' simultaneous
reservations; computing it on the client would allow double booking.

props.name: duration
props.description: Slot duration, already formatted: "30 min", "1 h".

props.name: resourceLabel
props.description: Resource name — room, hall, machine, advisor.

SplitAction.name: SplitAction
SplitAction.description:
A button with a primary action and a menu of related variants.

Exists for the case where one action has several forms that are used
rarely: "Send" on the button, and "Send as PDF" and "Save as draft" in the
menu. Not a replacement for `ActionGroup` — three equally-weighted actions
go in a group, not a menu.

Menu items are INTENTS, not free-form entries. An intent carries an icon, a
label, and a family; the label can be refined through `label`. That way the
menu cannot show an action that does not exist in `intents.ts`.

props.name: intent
props.description: The primary action. It sits on the button, not in the menu.

props.name: disabledReason
props.description: Why the primary action is disabled. The menu stays available.

props.name: menuLabel
props.description: Name of the button that opens the menu. Change it when "More actions" is not clear enough.

props.name: primary
props.description: Raises the main half to `filled`. The menu follows the same weight.

SplitPanel.name: SplitPanel
SplitPanel.description:
Two panels with a divider the user drags.

For a screen where two things are read together: a PDF on the left and the
form being filled from it on the right, a list beside a detail, a document
beside its journal entry.

The point is that the SPLIT is the user's decision. One person wants to see
the whole document, the next wants a wide form, and neither is wrong - so the
component holds a ratio rather than a fixed width.

props.name: defaultRatio
props.description: Starting share of the left panel, 0 to 1.

props.name: minRatio
props.description: How small either side may get, as a share. Stops a panel disappearing.

props.name: ratio
props.description: Controlled ratio. With it, `onRatioChange` is required.

StatCard.name: StatCard
StatCard.description: Change in percent relative to the previous period.

props.name: diff
props.description: Change in percent relative to the previous period.

props.name: invertDiff
props.description:
When `true`, a rise is shown in red and a drop in green.
For costs and debts, a rise is not good news.

StatGrid.name: StatGrid
StatGrid.description: Change in percent relative to the previous period.

props.name: maxColumns
props.description: Number of columns on the widest screens; capped at 4.

StatusBadge.name: StatusBadge
StatusBadge.description: Icon to the left of the text - useful when color alone carries meaning.

props.name: icon
props.description: Icon to the left of the text - useful when color alone carries meaning.

props.name: withBorder
props.description: Shows a border; useful on colored surfaces where the background doesn't contrast.

StatusScreen.name: StatusScreen
StatusScreen.description:
Shared base for interrupted screens: 404, 500, 503, suspended account,
maintenance.

Exists so these screens do not look like the default Next.js template. A
user who runs into an error should still see the product, not a blank
document with black text.

props.name: eyebrow
props.description: "404", "503" — label above the title.

props.name: linkComponent
props.description:
Component for links. Defaults to the one from `LiroAppProvider`.

Pass it manually only from client components — a function cannot cross
the server/client boundary, so `<NotFoundTemplate linkComponent={Link} />`
from `not-found.tsx` would break the build.

StepWizard.name: StepWizard
StepWizard.description:
Step wizard.

A pattern that repeats across several flows in Liro Business App —
signing a document, pairing a device, generating a filing. It is the same
everywhere: a sequence of steps in a modal, forward and back, then a final
success or error state.

Two rules the component enforces:

A step that runs on the server has no buttons. While waiting for a
response, "Back" would leave the record in a half-finished state, and
"Next" would have nothing to do.

The final state is not a step but an outcome. There is no going back from
success; the only way out is closing or a new action.

props.name: active
props.description: Index of the active step; controlled.

props.name: outcome
props.description: When set, the outcome is shown instead of the steps.

StockLedger.name: StockLedger
StockLedger.description:
Stock movement ledger.

The same display applies to a warehouse, fixed assets, a document archive,
and raw materials in production — in every case it is a sequence of
receipts and issues with a running balance.

The balance is NOT computed here. It comes from the server, because the
only correct balance is the one the database computed at the moment of the
movement; computing it on the client would drift as soon as pagination or a
filter appears.

props.name: itemLabel
props.description: Item name — article, equipment, raw material.

props.name: withBalance
props.description: Shows a column with the balance after each movement.

StructureTree.name: StructureTree
StructureTree.description:
Hierarchical structure.

An org chart, a product bill of materials, a chart of accounts, item
categories, rooms across buildings — all of these are trees where a node
carries a code, a name, and one number.

Indentation is drawn with lines, not just spacing: at a depth of four
levels, spacing alone stops showing which node belongs to which.

props.name: defaultExpandedDepth
props.description: Levels open on first display.

props.name: valueLabel
props.description: Label above the values column.

SuspendedTemplate.name: SuspendedTemplate
SuspendedTemplate.description:
Interrupted screens. All of them share the same frame from
`StatusScreen` — wordmark, icon in the status color, title, explanation,
one or two actions.

The texts explain what happened and what the user can do. They do not
apologize and do not use technical terms: "The page does not exist" is
more usable than "404 Not Found".

props.name: action
props.description: Overrides the default primary action.

props.name: linkComponent
props.description: Pass `next/link` so returning home stays client-side.

TableOfContents.name: TableOfContents
TableOfContents.description:
List of headings on the page, sticky to the side.

Tracks scroll position. This is not decoration — a list that only shows the
last CLICKED heading fails to answer the question it exists for: where am I
right now.

props.name: top
props.description: Offset from the top for the sticky position. Account for the header height.

props.name: trackScroll
props.description:
Tracks scroll position via `IntersectionObserver`.

Turn off when the headings from `items` are NOT on the page — in the
catalog, in an example, in the component's own documentation. In that
case the observer would look for an `id` that does not exist and the list
would be left with no active item.

TablePagination.name: TablePagination
TablePagination.description: When provided, shows the rows-per-page selector.

props.name: isFetching
props.description: Shows a discreet indicator while the next page is loading.

props.name: onPageSizeChange
props.description: When provided, shows the rows-per-page selector.

TargetBar.name: TargetBar
TargetBar.description:
Plan versus actuals.

Mantine's `BulletChart` draws three zones behind the bar with labels and
numbers on both sides; at card width that blurs into an unreadable strip.
This component is written from scratch with one goal: to show at a glance
whether the plan was met, and by how much it was missed.

The zones are quiet gray shades in the background — they are context, not
data. What carries color is the deviation from the target, because that is
the only reason this display is looked at in the first place.

props.name: caption
props.description: Extra data below: previous period, average, daily plan.

props.name: compact
props.description: Abbreviates large amounts on the axis: 1.2 M instead of 1,200,000.

props.name: currency
props.description: Currency code appended after the number, e.g. `RSD`.

props.name: decimals
props.description: Number of decimals; defaults to 0 on the axis, 2 with a currency.

props.name: invert
props.description: For expenses, an overshoot is bad news.

props.name: max
props.description: Upper bound of the axis; defaults to 125% of the target so an overshoot has room.

props.name: unit
props.description: Suffix for non-monetary values — `%`, `pcs`, `h`.

Toolbar.name: Toolbar
Toolbar.description:
Bar above the table: search on the left, filters next to it, actions on
the right.

Always the same layout, across all modules. Once the user knows where
search is on one screen, they know it on every next one.

props.name: actions
props.description: Actions on the right side — export, new entry.

props.name: filters
props.description: Selectors and buttons for filtering.

props.name: search
props.description: When passed, shows the search field.

TwoFactorCard.name: TwoFactorCard
TwoFactorCard.description:
Account and profile.

These screens exist in every application and are built from scratch
everywhere, so they end up slightly different everywhere. Here they are
components that receive values and return events — the application
decides what to do with them, the appearance is settled.

props.name: backupCodesLeft
props.description: Number of remaining backup codes; below three, a warning is shown.

TwoFactorForm.name: TwoFactorForm
TwoFactorForm.description:
Two-factor verification.

The code is submitted as soon as the last digit is entered — an extra
"Confirm" button is one press nobody needs. Pasting the code from an app
works because `PinInput` accepts the whole string at once.

props.name: length
props.description: Number of digits; TOTP is always 6, backup codes can be longer.

props.name: resendIn
props.description: Seconds until resend is allowed; the button is locked while it counts down.

UploadField.name: UploadField
UploadField.description: The storage path is saved, not the file itself.

props.name: value
props.description: The storage path is saved, not the file itself.

VersionCompare.name: VersionCompare
VersionCompare.description:
Comparison of two versions of a record.

A contract revision, a product spec change, a tax return correction, a
price list change — the question is always the same: what exactly changed.

Unchanged fields are hidden by default. A contract has forty fields, and
three changed; showing all forty means hiding those three among the rest.

props.name: beforeLabel
props.description: Label of the older version — "v3 · 12.03.2026."

props.name: showUnchanged
props.description: Hides unchanged fields; hidden by default.

WorkflowStatus.name: WorkflowStatus
WorkflowStatus.description:
Status flow of a record.

Shows where the record is and what comes next. Steps are described as data,
so the same piece of code draws invoice approval, a KYC check, and a
reservation path.

Horizontal for three to five steps in a header; vertical when the steps
carry an explanation or when there are more of them.

props.name: currentId
props.description: Id of the step the record is currently on.

props.name: states
props.description: Steps that were skipped or rejected — override the computed state.
